correctness.rationale: Ashikhmin--Barg Lemma 2.1 was inspected in the primary paper: minimal supports have size at most \(n-k+1\), minimal vectors span, and every nonminimal binary codeword splits into two nonzero disjoint-support subwords. The full gap therefore forces every minimal word to have weight \(d\); recursive splitting terminates and partitions any codeword into disjoint minimum words, proving divisibility. The intersection and odd-distance classification then follow exactly as stated. A fresh exhaustive replay through length seven and dimension three checked 17,140 subspaces, including 498 full-gap cases, with no counterexample.

correctness.rationale: Ashikhmin--Barg bounds every minimal support by \(n-k+1\) and gives a disjoint-support decomposition for every nonminimal binary word. The full initial gap therefore makes every minimal word minimum-weight, and induction partitions every codeword into disjoint minimum words, proving \(d\)-divisibility. The odd-distance classification follows because two distinct minimum words then cannot meet in \(d/2\) coordinates, so the spanning minimum words are pairwise disjoint. A compact exhaustive check confirms the conclusions for all binary codes of length at most six and dimension at most three.

originality.rationale: The recent mirror-band paper proves a local reflected vanishing interval, while the 1998 Ashikhmin--Barg paper supplies the classical ingredients. Targeted searches for the full-gap endpoint, equivalent all-minimal-words-at-minimum-weight formulations, divisibility, and odd-distance rigidity found no prior statement of the global closure theorem. Current archive searches by source identifier and claim family found no overlap. The assessment is only to the best of our knowledge, with material folklore and near-simultaneous priority risk.

value.rationale: The theorem converts a low-weight spectral gap into a global divisibility law for every codeword and yields a strong odd-distance obstruction: in dimension at least three the gap cannot reach \(n-k+1\). This gives a structural boundary complementary to the recent local mirror-vanishing theorem.
